q: Audibility means the ability to be heard or capability of detecting sounds in certain range of frequencies.
e: This is the exact textbook definition of audibility.

q: The range of frequencies a person can hear is known as the range of audibility.
e: This defines the specific frequency spectrum detectable by an individual.

q: For humans with normal hearing, the lower limit is 20 Hz and the upper limit is about 20 000 Hz.
e: These are the standard limits of human audibility.

q: For humans with normal hearing, the lower limit is 200 Hz and the upper limit is about 20 000 Hz.
e: The lower limit of human hearing is 20 Hz, not 200 Hz.

q: These limits are known as the limit of audibility.
e: The 20 Hz and 20 000 Hz boundaries are collectively called the limits of audibility.

q: Low frequency sounds which are under the lower limit of audibility (20 Hz) are called infrasound and cannot be heard by human.
e: Infrasound is defined by being below the human hearing threshold.

q: Low frequency sounds which are under the lower limit of audibility (20 Hz) are called ultrasound and cannot be heard by human.
e: Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound, whereas ultrasound refers to high frequencies.

q: A vibrating ruler can be seen but not heard its vibrating sound.
e: This is the textbook example used to illustrate infrasound.

q: This is because the sound produced is below the lower limit of audibility of human ear.
e: The slow vibration of a ruler produces infrasound.

q: High frequency sounds which are above the upper limit of audibility (20 000 Hz) are called ultrasound which cannot be heard by human ear.
e: This correctly defines ultrasound relative to human hearing.

q: Bats and whales use ultrasound in echolocation and most sonar technologies use ultrasound.
e: Both biological and technological echolocation primarily rely on ultrasound.

q: Bats and whales use infrasound in echolocation and most sonar technologies use infrasound.
e: They use ultrasound, not infrasound, for echolocation.

q: If you blow a dog whistle, a dog may bark in response, even though you do not hear any sound.
e: This is a common example of ultrasound application.

q: This is because the frequency of the sound produced by the whistle is above the upper limit of audibility of humans but within that of dogs.
e: Dogs have a higher upper limit of audibility than humans.

q: Manufacturers of concrete use ultrasound to check for cracks or cavities.
e: This is a listed industrial application of ultrasound quality control.

q: It can also be used to inspect metal pipes and measure the thickness of the wooden boards.
e: These are additional quality control applications of ultrasound mentioned in the text.

q: A prenatal ultrasound test uses high-frequency sound waves, inaudible to the human ear, that are transmitted through the abdomen via a device called a transducer.
e: This accurately describes the mechanism of prenatal ultrasound.

q: With prenatal ultrasound, the echoes are recorded and transformed into video or photographic images of the baby.
e: Echo interpretation is how ultrasound images are generated.

q: Ultrasonic scalers use ultrasound to remove calculus (plaque) deposits from the teeth.
e: This is a specific dental application of ultrasound.

q: They work mechanically using high frequency ultrasound that effectively blasts calculus.
e: The mechanical vibration is what removes the plaque.

q: The transmission of high energy ultrasound may result in the creation of cavitation bubbles.
e: Cavitation is a known physical effect of high-energy ultrasound.

q: Cavitation bubbles are created at sites of rarefaction.
e: The low-pressure phase of the sound wave (rarefaction) causes cavitation.

q: Cavitation bubbles are created at sites of compression.
e: Cavitation bubbles form during rarefaction, not compression.

q: These cavitation bubbles may displace contaminant from surfaces.
e: This displacement is the basis for ultrasonic cleaning.

q: Ultrasonic cleaning is especially effective in the cleaning of irregular surfaces or internal cavities and passageways.
e: Cavitation allows cleaning in areas that are hard to reach mechanically.

q: The sonar (sound navigation and ranging) is a type of technology that works based on echoes.
e: Sonar fundamentally relies on echo timing and interpretation.

q: It is used by the ships for navigation at sea and to detect the position of other vessels.
e: These are the primary maritime applications of sonar.

q: Infrasound waves have short wavelengths, and are thus unable to travel long distances.
e: Infrasound waves have long wavelengths, which allows them to travel long distances.

q: Infrasound waves which have lower frequency and longer wavelengths are able to travel longer distances with less attenuation.
e: This explains why animals like elephants use infrasound for long-distance communication.
